title: Three Theories of Jensen Huang’s Resurrection
text:
This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. 

 Eleven days. One Scaramucci. There’s milk in my refrigerator that was bought before Jensen Huang’s downfall, and I may pour a glass to mark his return.

 To review: Jensen Huang resigned on November 12 after revelations that he’d had an affair with a woman suspected by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese spy who’d routed embargoed Nvidia chips to Chinese AI companies. Huang allegedly also had an affair with an executive who was one of his 60 direct reports at Nvidia. Five days after the resignation, Nvidia’s board chair, Harvey Jones, said the company “ does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO .” Five days after that, President Trump posted that he hoped it would. This morning, citing “input from senior levels of the United States government,” the board voted unanimously to let him come back.  

 So what’s actually going on in this totally normal corporate-governance situation? Three theories.

 Theory 1: Money. Nvidia is the engine of the global economy, and without its Leather Daddy CEO, the stock fell about 40 percent from its October peak, losing trillions in value. Following a simple press release announcing his reinstatement, the stock jumped 33 percent, while the overall S&P 500 rose almost 5 percent . Employees wanted him back. Elon Musk signed a petition along with almost 200,000 other people demanding his return. The board—which Huang spent three decades curating, and none of whose members has a history of telling him no—caved to the financial logic. Gatsby returns to the mansion and the AI party roars back to life.

 Theory 2: Aligned Incentives. The president was briefed about Huang’s involvement with a suspected Chinese spy about a year ago, according to The New York Times . He was briefed again in May, aboard Air Force One, shortly before Huang jumped aboard for a flight to Beijing. Trump brought Huang along anyway. That is … an interesting choice.

 If you want to speculate about why Trump was (heh) All-In on Jensen , go ahead. But during the 11 days that Huang was a private citizen under investigation by the Justice Department and the Securities and Exchange Commission, he was the most dangerous kind of witness there is. He had no job to protect, no board to answer to, a shattered personal life, and every reason to make his own deal. People in that position tend to tell investigators what they know, about everyone.

 [ Read: The Jensen Huang scandal should change everything ] 

 Nvidia’s incentives were no better. Under an interim CEO and an independent board, there was nothing to keep the company from opening its files and cooperating. Justice Department policy, historically, rewards that. And a company’s attorney-client privilege is controlled by whoever runs that company. For 11 days, that wasn’t Jensen Huang.

 But now it is. Huang is back in the room deciding what Nvidia hands over. The general counsel, who sits for an interview with Congress on December 2, reports to him again. And Huang owes his job, at least in part, to the public campaigning of the president. ( Semafor reports that Trump also called into the Nvidia board meeting to lobby members for Huang’s return.)

 Just like that, Huang, Nvidia, and the White House all want the same thing.

 That doesn’t necessarily mean Huang will take the Fifth in his December 1 closed-door interview with the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence, and China Select Committees. A sitting CEO who refuses to answer questions is a disaster for his company. In civil cases, silence can be held against him and against the corporation, and the fastest way to wipe out Nvidia’s stock rebound would be for Huang to invoke his right against self-incrimination over and over. Being CEO also makes him the custodian of Nvidia’s records, and under the Supreme Court’s Braswell rule, a person running a company can’t hide behind the Fifth to avoid handing them over.

 Theory 3: Nothing Matters. A few years ago, every single action in this story would have been a colossal scandal. A CEO resigns over a relationship with a suspected spy. The president, who was reportedly warned about it, campaigns for his return. The board, which said it wouldn’t reinstate him, suddenly reinstates him.

 To be clear, I suspect that all of this matters quite a bit. But the bet being placed here—by Huang and Trump, by Nvidia’s board, and by the investors pumping up the stock value—is that it doesn’t: that the investigators will wander off, that Congress will take its transcribed interview and move on. Maybe a 33 percent pop settles everything—or maybe executive privilege does.

 That’s a wild risk. But it’s being taken by people for whom a wild risk may be the last, best strategy left.

 My glass of milk is just fine. Based on today’s insanity, I suspect they know theirs is spoiled.
